item.title: Xi lands in U.S. for state visit, greeted by Trump at airport
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan step out of the airplane cabin upon their arrival at Joint Base Andrews in the United States on Sept. 23, 2026. Xi arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon for a state visit to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi and Peng were warmly greeted by Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the airport in a rare planeside welcome. (Xinhua/Liu Bin) WASHINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon for a state visit to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, were warmly greeted by Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, at the airport in a rare planeside welcome. American children presented flowers to Xi and Peng. The honor guards lined up on both sides of the red carpet to pay their respects. The welcome ceremony also included a 21-gun salute, the playing of the national anthems of both countries and a military flyover. In a written speech, Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes to the U.S. people on behalf of the Chinese people. China and the United States are both great countries, and the two peoples are both great peoples, Xi said in the speech, adding that the two peoples have maintained friendly exchanges for a long time and their interests are deeply intertwined. China and the United States should be partners, not rivals, he said, noting that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, and that the two countries can help each other succeed and advance the well-being of the whole world. Xi noted that he and Trump agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability during Trump's visit to China in May, which has provided strategic guidance for the future development of bilateral ties. China and the United States should work in the same direction, promote a stable relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and promises of peace, Xi said. He said China and the United States, as two major countries, should find a right way to get along in the new era. Xi emphasized that the world is developing and times are changing, but the historical logic of peaceful coexistence between China and the United States has not changed, the goodwill of friendly exchanges between the two peoples has not changed, and the general expectations of the international community for China and the United States have not changed. Xi said he looks forward to having in-depth exchanges with Trump on major issues concerning bilateral relations and the world situation, constantly enriching the connotation of the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and expanding the space for exchanges and cooperation in various fields between the two countries. Xi said he also looks forward to engaging extensively with people from all walks of life in the United States to deepen friendship. With joint efforts, Xi said he believes the visit is sure to be fruitful, and will enhance the well-being of the two peoples and add hope for world peace. On Xi's way from the airport to his hotel by car, representatives of overseas Chinese and students gathered on both sides of the road, waving the national flags of China and the United States to warmly welcome his visit. ■ Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives at Joint Base Andrews on Sept. 23, 2026, for a state visit to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump. item.title: Young Chinese find roots, inspiration in Long March legacy
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Artists stage a Red Army-themed performance in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, June 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Xu Hongyan) GUIYANG, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- On stage, Red Army soldiers on the Long March braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and vast grasslands. Some fell amid a hail of gunfire, while others marched on to the end. When the performance ended and the lights came up, 24-year-old actor Tian Hongqiang found himself back in the present, witnessing a new China for all those who had sacrificed their lives. "I saw a glimmer of light shining in the audience's eyes. Grey-haired elders and young students in school uniforms gave us their thumbs-up," Tian said. "That makes me feel the power of the spirit we are trying to convey." For over two years, Tian has performed in "The Great Turning Point," a large-scale immersive production about the Long March being staged in Zunyi, southwest China's Guizhou Province. Known as China's "city of historic turning point," Zunyi holds a special place in the nation's history. In January 1935, during the Long March, the Communist Party of China (CPC) convened the Zunyi Meeting in a two-story building here at a critical historical crossroads. In October 1934, the CPC was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party (KMT). The setback was the result of left-leaning errors in military strategy and rigid Soviet-inspired dogmatism. The CPC-led Red Army fought its way across the Xiangjiang River in Guangxi and broke through the KMT troops' blockade, but suffered tens of thousands of casualties in the battle. The three-day meeting was thus convened to draw lessons. In the end, many key issues were resolved, including the establishment of a new Party leadership with Mao Zedong at the helm. Today, Zunyi is one of China's best-known destinations for historical education tours, which take visitors to sites associated with the country's revolutionary history. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. In Zunyi, the history that once unfolded in meeting rooms, mountain passes and battlefields is being retold via theater, immersive experiences and cultural products, drawing younger generations closer to the historical events. "The Great Turning Point," centered on the history of the Zunyi Meeting, premiered on Jan. 15, 2024, the meeting's 89th anniversary, and has staged more than 2,500 performances so far. Wang Liming, a marketing executive with the company behind the production, said about 60 percent of its audience are 25 to 50 years old, with many parents joining their children to watch. "We hope to help young people develop an emotional connection with this history, so that it is no longer just words and pictures in a textbook," Wang said. Among the audience was 10-year-old Xu Chen'en, who traveled from Chongqing Municipality in southwest China with her mother, Chen Jinghong. "I think the Red Army soldiers were very brave," Xu said. "We should learn from them and face our own difficulties courageously." Her mother sees the experience as a form of education that sinks in over time. "It is like planting a seed in her heart," Chen said. "She can experience the culture of the Long March now and gradually come to understand it as she grows up." For another visitor, surnamed Xia, the performance became an experience shared by three generations. She watched it with her 56-year-old aunt and 85-year-old grandmother. "My grandmother's generation has a strong emotional bond with this history, and she was deeply moved," Xia said. "For us, theater makes it much more immersive." The family's next stop was Loushan Pass, north of Zunyi, another landmark on the Long March route. After the Zunyi Meeting, the Red Army achieved a major victory there. What was once a battlefield is now a popular tourism destination. Twice a day, a live-action performance lasting nearly an hour recreates battle scenes. Roughly 90 performers are residents of nearby villages. "We want to make the spirit of the Long March something visitors can see and experience," said Zhu Jingbo, a local culture and tourism official. Visitors can take part in the performance, playing roles as local residents, helping to transport supplies and tending to wounded soldiers. Zhu said creators consulted historians while developing the show, including firsthand accounts of locals guiding Red Army troops across the region. This approach, he said, is intended to move beyond static museum displays, make revolutionary history more accessible to younger visitors, and create new opportunities for local communities. Around 15,000 students visit the Loushan Pass area each year on educational trips. Villagers who take part in performances can earn an additional 2,000 to 3,000 yuan (approximately 298 to 447 U.S. dollars) a month, depending on their roles. Such immersive experiences are part of a wider shift in China's revolutionary education tours. In recent years, historical education tours have increasingly diversified, with performances, study tours and cultural products complementing traditional visits to memorials and historic sites. China's plan for building the country into a tourism powerhouse during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) also calls for further exploring the historical and contemporary value of revolutionary heritage, improving exhibitions at revolutionary tourism sites, and expanding cultural products and performances. Thus the creative reinterpretation of the Long March spirit stretches far beyond museums and scenic spots. Zunyi's bustling downtown Red Army Street boasts a full range of Long March-themed cultural products, including figurines, backpacks and custom cups, making revolutionary culture accessible to younger audiences. Near the historical site of the Zunyi Meeting, designer Han Bing sells small Red Army figurines. He said many of his customers are students, particularly from primary and middle schools, while older visitors often buy the figurines as gifts for children. The shop, which opened in 2019, has maintained brisk business, with daily sales sometimes exceeding 12,000 yuan. For Han, the connection with the Long March is personal. He comes from Liping County in Guizhou, the first county seat reached by the Central Red Army after entering the province. Han grew up hearing a family story about a wooden bridge across the Bazhou River that Red Army troops once crossed. His great-grandfather, he said, helped build the bridge, which later became known locally as the "Red Army Bridge." Influenced by his family, Han developed an interest in revolutionary history at an early age and later studied art. Growing up during the early decades of China's reform and opening-up, he said he was initially fascinated by cultures from abroad. But when he started his own business and began exploring Chinese history and revolutionary culture more deeply, he felt as though he had found his roots. "I wanted to share that feeling with other people," Han said. "So I turned images of Red Army soldiers into figurines, using a form that younger people can relate to." When asked why the Long March should still be remembered 90 years later, he answered with a story from his own life. At the most difficult point in his entrepreneurial journey, Han said he had lost nearly all the money he had invested. Alone, he went to the top of Loushan Pass and recited a poem written there by Mao Zedong. "Fear not the strong pass iron-clad on all sides! The summit's now surmounted with big strides..." As he recited, he said his determination gradually returned. "What inspires me most is the enduring optimism of the Long March, the sense that hope never dies," Han said. "It's an inexhaustible source of strength." ■ This photo taken on Aug. 17, 2026 shows a view of Loushan Pass in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua/Shi Qiangui)

item.title: China's extended holiday set to boost long-haul travel, border crossings
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays bring travelers a major bonus this year: extra time for longer journeys and extended stays. Separated by three working days, the three-day and seven-day holiday periods can be bridged into a 13-day break running from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7. REACHING FAROFF DESTINATIONS For Shanghai white-collar worker Zheng Bing, the extended break means she can leave before the Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on Sept. 25 per the lunar calendar, and spend more time in Malaysia. "This allows me to enjoy my vacation at a leisurely pace," said Zheng, whose plans mirror a wider desire for long-haul travel over the coming holiday. Data from Chinese online travel platforms show that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular, making up 26 percent of all bookings. Meanwhile, flight reservations for top international destinations have surged over 20 percent year on year. "Sales for international packages with stays over 10 days are up from last year," said Wang Wei, president of the Shanghai-based Spring International Travel Service (Group) Co., Ltd. Popular spots include Spain, Greece, Britain, Türkiye and Azerbaijan, the firm added. China's National Immigration Administration expects an average of about 2.25 million cross-border trips per day during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday from Sept. 25 to 27, and about 2.15 million per day during the National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7. Sales of tour packages to domestic long-haul destinations are also gaining momentum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, reservations to such destinations, including Urumqi in northwest China's Xinjiang, Kunming in southwest Yunnan, and Sanya in the far southern island province of Hainan, have been on the rise. Flight ticket bookings confirm this trend. According to data from Umetrip, a mobile platform for real-time flight information, the number of reservations for domestic flights flying over 2,000 km surpassed 1.74 million, a year-on-year increase of 14 percent. EXPERIENCES OUTWEIGH CHECKLIST TOURS Analysts said that more tourists are favoring special travel experiences, niche tourist destinations and customized packages, particularly when the upcoming super-long holiday makes such travel plans easier to enjoy. "For younger tourists, how to spend a vacation matters more than where to spend it," said Yang Han, a researcher with online travel platform Qunar. In the upcoming holidays, bookings for glacier hiking on Fliggy went up 50 percent from the previous year, skydiving up nearly 80 percent, and whale watching surged 200 percent. Niche tourist destinations, such as lesser-known county-level towns, are attracting tourists. Online travel platform Tongcheng predicted that tourists will stay 3.2 days longer in county-level destinations on average compared with the same period last year. Tourists are also discovering new sides of cities and towns beyond their famous landmarks or cultural heritage. On online travel platforms, hotel bookings and ticket reservations have surged in cities hosting concerts, sporting events and cultural activities. QUALITY TOUR PACKAGES IN DEMAND As more tourists opt for immersive, in-depth experiences rather than hurried sightseeing, they are also on the hunt for better accommodation and higher-quality travel services. A longer holiday creates more room for tourism consumption, said Cheng Chaogong at Tongcheng. "Quality and experience will become key factors," Cheng noted. The government is also on the move to make sure diverse cultural events and spending incentives are in place across the country. China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign on Sept. 22. While hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, local governments are handing out some 310 million yuan (about 45.9 million U.S. dollars) in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption. Zheng is about to leave for Malaysia tonight. She's eagerly anticipating her unhurried but fulfilling holiday. "I could still have time to take a rest and check the air of festivity in Shanghai after the trip," she said. ■

item.title: Service consumption outpaces goods as China's consumer market enters new stage: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market has entered a new stage in which goods and services are both important, with service retail sales expanding at nearly five times the pace of goods retail sales in the first eight months of this year, a structural shift captured by a new official indicator in the world's second-largest consumer market. Total retail sales of consumer goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year in the January-August period this year, with service retail sales up 4.9 percent and goods retail sales up 1 percent, officials and experts said at the China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk platform hosted by Xinhua News Agency. In June this year, the National Bureau of Statistics released the "total retail sales of consumer goods and services" indicator for the first time, a move analysts say better reflects the full picture of consumption as services become an increasingly important driver of domestic demand. "As per capita income rises, it is an objective economic law that service consumption grows faster than goods consumption," said Lin Jian, vice president of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce. The shift is visible in changing consumer behavior. Zhang Weihua, deputy director of the Shandong Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism, said consumers are moving from "buying goods" to "buying peace of mind" and from "functional consumption" to "experiential consumption," seeking immersive, interactive and emotionally rewarding experiences. For his part, Chen Chunhui, chairman of Xiamen International Cruise Home Port Group Co., Ltd., said that "cruise consumption, from ship to shore, integrates dining, lodging, transport, sightseeing, shopping and entertainment, reflecting the growing demand for composite experiences." In Xiamen, a coastal city in east China's Fujian Province, the Xiamen International Cruise Home Port, one of China's four pilot demonstration cruise transport ports, saw inbound cruise ship calls rise 33 percent year on year in the first half, with passenger numbers up about 180 percent, according to Chen. "In the long run, sustainable consumption growth hinges on a virtuous cycle between consumption upgrading and industrial upgrading, with demand-side policies pushing manufacturers toward greener and smarter production," Lin said. On the policy front, China has been steering demand toward green and smart products through trade-in programs for automobiles and home appliances. The leverage ratio of subsidy funds rose from 1:7.8 in 2025 to 1:10.3 this year, according to Lin. China is the world's second-largest consumer market. The country targets relatively fast growth in total consumer goods and services consumption, with total retail sales of consumer goods reaching around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.3 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030. It also aims to cultivate 10-trillion-yuan-level markets in green, intelligent and health-related consumption. China also aims to attract 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars, according to a new five-year tourism development plan unveiled in July this year. The plan signals the country's expanding efforts to draw overseas visitors as it seeks to boost consumption. Lin said new growth areas such as "AI plus consumption" are expected to expand rapidly, providing broad space for the upgrading of goods and services consumption. "Service consumption and goods consumption will become more deeply integrated, with their boundaries increasingly blurred. But what remains unchanged is starting from user demand and continuously turning real needs into products," said Zhang Dandan, head of the Changsha New Consumption Research Institute. "During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China's service consumption is expected to accelerate further," Lin added. ■

item.title: Quotable Quotes: Xi Jinping on family and country
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-24
Friday marks the Mid-Autumn Festival, also known as the Moon Festival, a traditional Chinese holiday when families gather to celebrate. Under the full moon, people share mooncakes and savor the joy of reunion. The moon goddess Chang'e, the Jade Rabbit, the osmanthus tree and glowing lanterns are among the timeless symbols of the festival. In Chinese culture, love for one's family is closely tied to a sense of responsibility for the country. President Xi Jinping has often spoken about this connection. Let's revisit his words and the values they reflect. ■

(Xinhua/Zhang Tao) BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- People across China on Wednesday held various activities to celebrate the ninth Chinese farmers' harvest festival. The festival is the first national festival created specifically for the country's farmers. This year's festival falls on Wednesday. Launched in 2018, the festival coincides with the Autumnal Equinox each year, which is one of the 24 solar terms of the Chinese lunisolar calendar and usually falls between Sept. 22 and 24 during the country's agricultural harvest season.
